content: The optimal proportion of dietary energy derived from fat and its impact on body weight remain unclear. To address the prevention of overweight and obesity in the general population, it is essential to understand the relationship between fat-derived energy intake and body fatness. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of fat intake on body fatness measures, including body weight, waist circumference, body fat percentage, and body mass index (BMI), in adults not actively attempting to lose weight. The analysis was based on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) lasting at least six months. A comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, up to October 2019. No language restrictions were applied. Eligible trials included adults aged 18 years or older, randomized to either a lower-fat or higher-fat diet, without any intention to induce weight loss. Multifactorial interventions were excluded, and only trials assessing body fatness measures after at least six months were considered. Inclusion decisions were made independently by multiple reviewers, with disagreements resolved through discussion or consultation with a third party. Data extraction was performed in duplicate, focusing on population characteristics, interventions, controls, and outcomes. Body fatness measures, including body weight, BMI, body fat percentage, and waist circumference, were independently extracted at all available time points. Statistical analyses included random-effects meta-analyses, meta-regression, subgroup analyses, sensitivity analyses, funnel plot assessments, and GRADE evaluations. The review included 37 RCTs involving 57,079 participants. High-quality evidence consistently demonstrated that reducing total fat intake led to modest reductions in body fatness. This effect was observed across nearly all included studies and remained robust in sensitivity analyses. Specifically, a lower-fat diet resulted in an average body weight reduction of 1.4 kg (95% confidence interval [CI]: -1.7 to -1.1 kg) based on data from 26 RCTs involving 53,875 participants (I² = 75%). Subgroup analyses and meta-regression indicated that greater weight loss was associated with larger reductions in fat intake, lower baseline fat consumption, and higher baseline BMI. The effect on weight did not diminish over time and was accompanied by reductions in BMI (mean difference [MD]: -0.5 kg/m², 95% CI: -0.6 to -0.3), waist circumference (MD: -0.5 cm, 95% CI: -0.7 to -0.2), and body fat percentage (MD: -0.3%, 95% CI: -0.6 to 0.0, p = 0.05). These findings were based on data from 14, 3, and 2 trials, respectively, with low heterogeneity (I² = 21% or 0%). No evidence suggested that low-fat diets caused harm that could offset their benefits on body fatness. Additionally, reductions in body weight were associated with small decreases in low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol (-0.13 mmol/L, 95% CI: -0.21 to -0.05) and total cholesterol (-0.23 mmol/L, 95% CI: -0.32 to -0.14). There was minimal or no effect on high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol (-0.02 mmol/L, 95% CI: -0.03 to 0.00), triglycerides (0.01 mmol/L, 95% CI: -0.05 to 0.07), systolic blood pressure (-0.75 mmHg, 95% CI: -1.42 to -0.07), or diastolic blood pressure (-0.52 mmHg, 95% CI: -0.95 to -0.09). These findings were supported by high-quality evidence. Quality of life was minimally affected (MD: 0.04, 95% CI: 0.01 to 0.07 on a 0-to-10 scale), with low-quality evidence. In conclusion, RCTs comparing lower-fat diets to higher-fat diets, without the intention of weight loss, consistently demonstrated small but stable reductions in body fatness, including body weight, BMI, waist circumference, and body fat percentage. Greater reductions in fat intake, lower baseline fat consumption, and higher baseline BMI were associated with more pronounced weight loss. There was no evidence of harm to serum lipids, blood pressure, or quality of life, and small benefits were observed in some parameters.
